one_liner: Header-only C++23 coroutine fork-join task library with a work-stealing pool; roughly ties oneTBB, beats OpenMP tasks.
what_it_does: Coros turns functions into tasks by returning coros::Task<T> and using co_return/co_await; tasks run on a coros::ThreadPool started with start_sync/start_async from main. Tasks wait on children with co_await coros::wait_tasks(...) (lazy scheduling) or wait_tasks_async (eager), fire-and-forget with enqueue_tasks, and chain with chain_tasks(...).and_then(...). Results and exceptions are stored in std::expected<T, std::exception_ptr>. It is a new API, not a drop-in for TBB parallel_invoke or OpenMP task pragmas.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker owns a Chase-Lev work-stealing deque (circular power-of-two buffer, grown 4x on overflow, after Le et al.'s correct weak-memory-model deque) storing coroutine handles; idle workers pick a random victim and scan all queues, then fall back to a shared moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue for tasks submitted from outside. Stackless coroutines make a spawn a heap-allocated coroutine frame plus a deque push, and co_await on a child uses symmetric transfer so nested waits do not grow the stack. top_ and bottom_ are padded with hardware_destructive_interference_size to avoid false sharing.
when_to_use: C++23 code (GCC 13+ or Clang 17+) that wants fork-join recursion expressed with co_await instead of TBB lambdas or OpenMP pragmas
Very fine-grained recursive tasks (fib-style spawn trees) where OpenMP tasks, especially GCC libgomp, are orders of magnitude slower per the README graphs
Small codebases that want a vendorable, header-only, BSL-1.0 scheduler with exception propagation via std::expected
Moving work between several thread pools (wait_tasks(tp, ...) resumes the awaiting task on a named pool)
when_not_to_use: If oneTBB is already in use: the README graphs show parity on x86 (Coros ~27 ms vs oneTBB ~25 ms for fib(30) at 16 threads) and only modest wins on ARM
Latency- or power-sensitive processes: idle workers busy-spin forever (run() loops on noop_coroutine; thread yielding is a TODO), burning 100% CPU on every pool thread
MSVC builds (not supported) or toolchains without std::expected
Clang on x86 at high steal rates: open issue #2 reports the seq_cst atomic_thread_fence in Dequeue::steal() compiles to mfence and dominates matmul time
Long-lived pools with bursty spawning: grown deque buffers are kept in old_buffers_ until the pool is destroyed

integration.min_toolchain: C++23, GCC 13+ (with -fcoroutines) or Clang 17+ (libc++); MSVC not supported
integration.platforms: x86-64 and ARM per the README graphs; any platform with C++23 threads and atomics otherwise not documented
integration.thread_safety: ThreadPool is shared by its workers; tasks from outside go through a lock-free MPMC queue; the pool must outlive its tasks. CI runs ASan and TSan builds.

gotchas: Exceptions thrown inside enqueue_tasks tasks are rethrown immediately, since nothing awaits them; Task<void> has no value()/operator*
Lambda coroutines with captures are unsafe once the lambda dies; pass state through coroutine parameters

Published harness flaw: benchmarks/tbb/fib_tbb.h and mat_tbb.h hard-code tbb::task_arena arena(4) and ignore g_thread_num, so the committed oneTBB benchmark always runs 4 threads; the oneTBB thread sweep in the README graphs cannot be reproduced from the repo as committed

Each harness writes 50 millisecond-resolution runs per thread count to text files; how the plotted value was derived (mean, median) is not documented, and the TBB matmul uses std::atomic<int> inputs where Coros uses plain int
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The other coroutines-fibers entries (minicoro, libaco, libco-style switchers, Boost.Cobalt) are context-switch or async I/O primitives; pick Coros when you need a parallel fork-join scheduler on stackless C++ coroutines, and Marl when you need stackful fibers that may block.
verified_claims_summary: README graphs (read by eye) show fib(30) time vs threads (1-16) and a 1024x1024 recursive int matmul against oneTBB, GCC libgomp and LLVM libomp: at 16 threads x86 fib Coros ~27 ms vs oneTBB ~25 ms, libomp ~140 ms, libgomp ~3000 ms; ARM fib ~22 ms vs ~27 ms oneTBB; matmul ~818 ms vs ~840 ms oneTBB. Benchmark CMake uses -std=c++23 -O3 (-fcoroutines -fopenmp for GCC, libc++ and libomp for Clang); compiler versions and CPU models are not stated, and the committed oneTBB harness pins 4 threads.
status_note: Stale since 2024-09-13 with one open performance issue (#2); BSL-1.0 and header-only, so easy to vendor, but treat it as a well-built student-scale scheduler rather than a TBB replacement.
